speaker: Doctor
text:
Thank you for your patience. To begin our assessment, how old is the child, and how long have these skin lesions been present?

REQUEST TEST: Complete_Blood_Count
REQUEST TEST: Liver_Function_Tests

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Complete_Blood_Count: WBC 6,000 /μL, Hemoglobin 12 g/dL, Platelets 300,000 /μL; Liver_Function_Tests: NORMAL READINGS

speaker: Doctor
text: The blood work and liver function tests appear normal. Do these lesions itch, bleed, or change color, and do you have any fever or recent insect bites?

speaker: Patient
text: 2-year-old female. The patient's mother reports noticing multiple painless, nonpruritic papules on the child's abdomen. The child attends daycare where another child was reported to have similar lesions recently. Patient's brother had chickenpox one month ago. Immunizations are up-to-date.

speaker: Doctor
text:
Thank you for the details; the daycare exposure and normal labs are helpful clues. Since these are painless papules in a child, have you noticed any scaling on the lesions, and does the child have a fever or runny nose? Also, does the child have a history of atopy or eczema?

REQUEST IMAGES: Close-up of skin lesions

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Skin-colored, nontender, pearly papules with central umbilication on the abdomen and extremities.

speaker: Doctor
text: DIAGNOSIS READY: Molluscum Contagiosum. The description of skin-colored, pearly papules with central umbilication is pathognomonic for this viral infection, which is highly contagious in daycare settings. Given the up-to-date immunizations and normal CBC, no further testing or immediate treatment is required.
